Nerve Transmission. The propagation of electrical and chemical signals along neurons, enabling rapid communication throughout the nervous system. The process relies on ion gradients maintained across the cell membrane—high potassium inside, high sodium outside—and on gated ion channels that open and close in response to voltage changes. An electrical impulse called an action potential travels along the axon at high speed. At the synapse, the impulse triggers neurotransmitter release, which bridges the gap to the next neuron, regenerating the electrical signal downstream. This mechanism underlies all sensation, movement, and thought.

The resting potential, typically negative seventy millivolts, arises from the sodium-potassium pump maintaining a concentration gradient. Inside the cell, roughly 140 millimolar potassium and 10 millimolar sodium. Outside, roughly 5 millimolar potassium and 145 millimolar sodium. Depolarization begins when a stimulus opens sodium channels. Sodium floods in, driving the membrane voltage positive, reaching peak depolarization at about positive 30 millivolts.

The action potential is a stereotyped all-or-nothing voltage spike. Depolarization opens more sodium channels in positive feedback. Then inactivation gates close sodium channels while delayed potassium channels open, allowing potassium efflux to restore negative voltage. The refractory period prevents backward signal propagation. Sodium channels remain inactivated for roughly two milliseconds in absolute refractory period, making the neuron temporarily unresponsive. Potassium channels remain open slightly longer in relative refractory period, hyperpolarizing the neuron and requiring stronger stimuli to fire again.

Propagation along the axon is fastest in myelinated axons, where myelin insulation formed by glial cells allows voltage changes to depolarize distant segments directly, jumping between nodes of Ranvier at speeds up to 120 meters per second. Synaptic transmission converts electrical signals to chemical. The action potential opens calcium channels at the axon terminal. Calcium influx triggers exocytosis of neurotransmitter-filled vesicles into the synaptic cleft. Neurotransmitter molecules bind receptors on the postsynaptic cell, opening ion channels there and either exciting or inhibiting the downstream neuron. Each synapse sums these excitatory and inhibitory inputs, determining whether the postsynaptic neuron fires.
